What is your ARN, and is it currently valid?
How are you paid on what you are suggesting?
Does my money go directly to the fund house?
Will the units be in my own name?

## SIP Calculator: Estimate Your Monthly SIP Returns | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/sip-calculator

Enter a monthly amount, a time period and an assumed return to see what a SIP could grow to. It shows how much you put in and how much is illustrated growth. Try your numbers
Monthly SIP ₹
Time period years
Assumed return % a year
Illustrated future value —
This is an illustration that assumes the same return every year. Real returns go up and down and are not guaranteed. The 12% starting value is only an example, not a forecast.
What a monthly SIP can look like
Illustrative values at an assumed 12% a year, with a contribution at the start of each month:
Monthly SIP 10 years 15 years 20 years 25 years
₹1,000 ₹2.24 L ₹4.76 L ₹9.20 L ₹17.02 L
₹5,000 ₹11.20 L ₹23.80 L ₹45.99 L ₹85.11 L
₹10,000 ₹22.40 L ₹47.59 L ₹91.99 L ₹1.70 Cr
₹25,000 ₹56.01 L ₹1.19 Cr ₹2.30 Cr ₹4.26 Cr
The formula behind it
The calculator converts the yearly return to an equivalent monthly rate, i = (1 + r) 1/12 − 1 , then calculates:
Future value = P × [((1 + i) n − 1) ÷ i] × (1 + i)
Here P is the monthly SIP and n is the number of months. Some other calculators use r ÷ 12 as the monthly rate, so their answers can be slightly higher.
What moves the result most
Time: later years add more because earlier growth is also growing.
Amount: doubling the SIP doubles the illustrated value.
Return: a small change compounds over time, so also try a lower return to see a more cautious picture.

## How to Start a SIP in India: Steps & Documents
Source: https://moneytec.in/how-to-start-sip

A SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) invests a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly. Many schemes accept SIPs from ₹500 a month, and most can be changed or stopped later. Six steps to your first SIP
Name the goal. Decide what the money is for and roughly when you will need it.
Choose a comfortable amount. Start with what you can keep paying in a difficult month. You can raise it as your income grows. The SIP calculator helps you compare amounts.
Complete KYC. KYC is done once and works across fund houses, mostly online.
Understand the scheme. Read about its risk level, costs, any exit load and the scheme documents.
Set up the auto-debit. Choose a date soon after your salary and approve the bank mandate.
Review it. Check in about once a year, or when your goal or income changes.
Documents you usually need
PAN
Aadhaar (or a passport for NRIs)
A bank account in your name
A photo
Common mistakes
Choosing an amount you cannot sustain, then stopping early.
Investing money you may need soon in a scheme that can fall in value.
Choosing a scheme only because of its recent returns. Past performance may not continue.
Forgetting about lock-ins. ELSS funds lock each instalment for 3 years.
A SIP makes investing regular. It does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in falling markets.

## NRI Mutual Fund Investment in India: NRE & NRO Guide
Source: https://moneytec.in/nri-mutual-fund-investment

Yes, NRIs can invest in Indian mutual funds, including through SIPs. Investments are made through an NRE or NRO account in rupees. Residents of the US and Canada can invest with select fund houses only. NRE or NRO account?
NRE account NRO account
Typically used for Money earned outside India Income earned in India, such as rent or pension
Taking money back abroad Generally freely repatriable Repatriable within limits, subject to rules and paperwork
Which one suits you depends on where the money came from and whether you may want to move it abroad later. Check the current rules with your bank before you invest.
Documents you usually need
PAN
Passport, and overseas address proof
NRE or NRO bank account details
A photo
FATCA details about your tax residency
KYC requirements can differ between fund houses, and some steps can be completed online.
If you live in the US or Canada
Only select fund houses accept investments from residents of the US and Canada, and they may ask for extra declarations. Check which ones accept you before you choose a scheme. Gulshan will tell you which fund houses are available for you.
Tax
Gains can be taxed in India, tax may be deducted at source, and your country of residence may also tax them. A double-taxation agreement may help. Ask a tax professional who knows both countries, as rules change and depend on your situation.
Investing from abroad
A monthly SIP can run from your NRE or NRO account. You do not need to be in India for each instalment. You can use the SIP calculator to compare amounts in rupees; currency movements can change what those rupees are worth to you abroad.

## ELSS Funds: Lock-in, Tax Rules & SIPs | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/elss-tax-saving-funds

An ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) is an equity mutual fund with a 3-year lock-in. Under the old tax regime, investments have been eligible for a deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh a year, popularly known as the Section 80C benefit. The key points
Lock-in: 3 years from the date of each investment.
Tax deduction: available under the old tax regime, within the overall ₹1.5 lakh yearly limit. It is not available under the new regime.
Risk: ELSS funds invest mainly in equities, so their value can fall and returns are not guaranteed.
How the lock-in works with a SIP
Each SIP instalment has its own 3-year lock-in. It does not all unlock together.
Instalment invested Can be redeemed from
January 2027 January 2030
February 2027 February 2030
March 2027 March 2030
A lump sum, by contrast, is locked for 3 years from the one date you invested.
Questions to ask yourself first
Which tax regime do you use? Under the new regime there is no ELSS deduction, so tax saving is not a reason to choose it.
Have you already used your ₹1.5 lakh limit through EPF, PPF, life insurance premiums or home-loan principal?
Can you leave the money invested for at least 3 years, and ideally longer, given the equity risk?
Income-tax law and section numbers change. Confirm the current rules and your own position with a tax professional before you invest for a deduction. Gains on redemption may also be taxable.

## What Is a Mutual Fund? Types, NAV & Risks | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/what-is-mutual-fund

A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in shares, bonds or other assets, as set out in the scheme’s stated objective. A professional fund manager runs it, and each investor owns units in proportion to what they put in. How a mutual fund works
You invest money in a scheme, either in one go or through a SIP .
You receive units based on that day’s price per unit, called the NAV.
The fund manager invests the pooled money according to the scheme’s objective.
The value of your units changes as the value of the investments changes.
You redeem units when you need the money, subject to the scheme’s terms.
A simple example
Suppose you invest ₹10,000 when the NAV is ₹50. You receive 200 units. If the NAV later rises to ₹60, your units are worth ₹12,000. If it falls to ₹40, they are worth ₹8,000. These numbers are only an illustration.
Main types of mutual funds
SEBI groups open-ended schemes into five broad categories:
Type What it mainly invests in General risk character
Equity funds Company shares Higher ups and downs; usually for longer periods
Debt funds Bonds and money-market instruments Usually steadier than equity, but not risk-free
Hybrid funds A mix of equity and debt Depends on the mix
Solution-oriented funds Built for goals such as retirement or children’s needs Depends on the portfolio; may have a lock-in
Other funds Index funds, ETFs and funds of funds Depends on what they track or hold
ELSS funds are a type of equity fund with a 3-year lock-in.
What it costs
Expense ratio: a yearly cost, taken from the fund’s assets, that is already reflected in the NAV.
Exit load: a charge some schemes apply if you redeem within a set period.
Tax: gains can be taxed when you redeem. The rules depend on the fund type and how long you held it.
The risks
Mutual funds do not guarantee returns or protect your capital. Market movements, interest rates, credit quality and how long you stay invested can all affect the result. Every scheme shows a riskometer, from Low to Very High, so read that and the scheme documents before you invest.
Who protects investors?
Mutual funds in India are regulated by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India). Your money is held by an independent custodian and trustees oversee the fund house, which is separate from your distributor. AMFI is the industry body that registers distributors. Regulation does not remove market risk.
Read next
What is a SIP? Mutual fund terms explained Mutual fund KYC

## What Is a SIP? How It Works, SIP vs Lump Sum | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/what-is-sip

A SIP, or Systematic Investment Plan, is a way to invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually every month. It is not a separate product; it is a way of putting money into a mutual fund scheme. How a SIP works
You pick a scheme, an amount and a date.
You approve an auto-debit from your bank.
On each date, the amount goes to the fund house and you receive units at that day’s NAV.
Your units add up over time, and you can change or stop the SIP later.
Rupee cost averaging: a worked example
Because the amount stays fixed, you buy more units when the NAV is lower and fewer when it is higher. Here is ₹1,000 a month for three months, with made-up NAVs:
Month Invested NAV Units bought
1 ₹1,000 ₹10.00 100
2 ₹1,000 ₹8.00 125
3 ₹1,000 ₹12.50 80
Total ₹3,000 Average cost ₹9.84 305
The average cost per unit (₹9.84) is below the simple average of the three NAVs (₹10.17). This averages your buying price over time, but it does not guarantee a profit or prevent a loss.
SIP or lump sum?
SIP Lump sum
How you invest A fixed amount at regular intervals One larger amount at once
Suits Regular income Money you already have
Timing Spread across many dates Depends on one entry date
Neither is always better. In a steadily rising market, a lump sum can do better because the money is invested for longer.
Ways to run a SIP
Regular SIP: the same amount each month.
Step-up SIP: the amount rises at set intervals, for example when your income grows. Where offered, it is a simple way to keep up with a goal.
Pause: many fund houses let you pause for a limited time. Terms vary.
Three common myths
“SIPs always make money.” No. A SIP in a scheme whose value falls can show a loss.
“I am locked in.” Usually not, except ELSS, where each instalment is locked for 3 years.
“I need a large amount.” Many schemes start at ₹500 a month.
Next steps
How to start a SIP SIP calculator The power of compounding

## The Power of Compounding Explained with Examples | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/power-of-compounding

Compounding means your returns can start earning returns of their own. Over a short period the effect looks small. Over a long period, it can do more of the work than the money you put in. The verse on our homepage
जलबिन्दुनिपातेन क्रमशः पूर्यते घटः । स हेतुः सर्वविद्यानां धर्मस्य च धनस्य च ॥
Drop by drop, a pot fills. In the same way, steady effort builds knowledge, virtue and wealth. It is the idea behind a monthly SIP: small amounts, repeated patiently.
₹1 lakh, left alone
Illustration at an assumed constant 12% a year, with no further investment:
After Illustrated value
10 years ₹3.11 L
20 years ₹9.65 L
30 years ₹29.96 L
The second 10 years add much more than the first, because growth is now being earned on a larger amount.
Why starting early matters
₹5,000 a month at an assumed 12% a year:
Years invested You put in Illustrated value
15 ₹9.00 L ₹23.80 L
25 ₹15.00 L ₹85.11 L
35 ₹21.00 L ₹2.76 Cr
Try your own numbers in the SIP calculator .
The Rule of 72
Divide 72 by a yearly return to estimate how long money takes to double. At 12%, that is about 6 years; at 6%, about 12 years. It is a rough mental shortcut.
What can get in the way
Stopping early: the biggest growth tends to come in the later years.
Inflation: a larger number in future will buy less than it does today.
Market falls: real returns are uneven and can be negative for a long time.
Costs and tax: these reduce what stays invested.
All figures here assume a constant return before costs and tax. Real investments do not grow in a straight line, and these are not promises of future returns.

## Goal-Based Investing: Plan a Monthly SIP | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/goal-based-investing

Goal-based investing starts with what the money is for: a child’s education, a home, retirement. You estimate what it could cost then, how long you have, and how much to set aside. This is how our goal planner on the homepage works. Four steps
Name the goal and today’s cost.
Set the timeline: the year you will need the money.
Allow for inflation: most goals cost more later.
Work out the monthly amount, counting what you have already saved for it.
A worked example
A goal that costs ₹25 lakh today, 15 years away, with 6% inflation, an assumed 12% yearly return and no existing savings:
Step Illustrated result
Cost today ₹25 lakh
Cost after 15 years at 6% inflation ₹59.91 L
Monthly SIP at an assumed 12% a year About ₹12,600
Try your own goal in the goal planner .
Timeline shapes the plan
Timeline Typical goals What to think about
3–5 years Emergency fund, short-term goals Access to your money, exit conditions and capital risk
5–10 years A car, a wedding, a home down-payment Your target, timeline and a comfortable monthly amount
10–30+ years Retirement, children’s education, long-term wealth Affordability, inflation and your ability to stay invested
These are starting points for a conversation, not product recommendations.
As the goal gets closer
A market fall matters more when you need the money soon. Many investors review their plan each year and consider moving towards less volatile options as the date nears, so the goal is less exposed to a late fall.
Why not just invest without a goal?
It gives you a number to work towards, instead of a guess.
It helps you match your risk to your timeline.
You are less tempted to spend money that has a job to do.
Inflation and returns here are assumptions. Your real costs and returns will differ, so review your plan regularly.

## What Is Life Insurance? Term Plans & Claims | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/what-is-life-insurance

Life insurance is a contract: you pay a premium, and if the insured person dies during the policy term, the insurer pays the agreed amount to the nominee, subject to the policy terms. It is meant to protect the people who depend on your income. The main types
Type What it does Good to know
Term insurance Pays a death benefit during the term Usually gives high cover for the premium; standard plans pay nothing if you outlive the term
Endowment and savings plans Combine cover with a maturity benefit Higher premium; compare the benefits carefully
ULIPs Combine cover with market-linked investment Have charges, market risk and a lock-in
Whole-life plans Provide cover for most of your life Terms vary by plan
How much cover might you need?
A common way to think about it, before you get a personal assessment, is to add up what your family would need:
Household expenses for the years they would depend on your income
Outstanding loans, such as a home loan
Future goals, such as children’s education
Then subtract existing cover and savings that could be used. The right cover also depends on affordability, health and eligibility.
Before you buy
Tell the insurer everything: health, smoking, occupation and existing policies. Non-disclosure can affect a claim.
Read the exclusions: know what the policy does not cover.
Name your nominee and tell your family that the policy exists.
Check the premium period and what happens if you miss a payment.
Use the free-look period: you can review the policy after you receive it and return it within the stated period, subject to its terms.
How a claim generally works
The nominee informs the insurer.
They submit the claim form, death certificate, policy and identity documents.
The insurer reviews the claim under the policy terms and decides.
How Moneytec can help
Gulshan Kohli is a Kotak Life advisor (KLI61205587). You can explore life cover through Kotak Life with him, subject to eligibility, underwriting and policy terms. He helps you list existing policies, dependants, commitments and loans, and discuss cover, exclusions and affordability before you choose. Premiums go to the insurer, not to Moneytec.
Insurance is the subject matter of solicitation. For more details on risk factors, terms and conditions, read the sales brochure and policy document carefully before concluding a sale.

## What Is Health Insurance? Cashless & Waiting Periods
Source: https://moneytec.in/what-is-health-insurance

Health insurance helps pay medical costs when you are treated for a covered illness or injury, usually in hospital, up to the amount you are insured for. You pay a premium, typically every year, and the insurer pays eligible costs under the policy terms. Why it is different from life insurance
Life insurance protects your family if you die. Health insurance helps pay for treatment while you are alive. Many families look at both when planning for the unexpected.
Two common ways to set up cover
Individual policy Family floater
Cover Each person has their own sum insured The family shares one sum insured
Think about Older members or specific health needs One large claim can use up cover for everyone that year
How claims work
Cashless: at a network hospital, the insurer settles approved costs directly with the hospital.
Reimbursement: you pay first, then claim the eligible amount from the insurer with your bills and documents.
Terms worth understanding
Term Meaning
Sum insured The most the policy pays in a policy year, subject to its terms
Waiting period Time before some conditions are covered, such as pre-existing illnesses
Room rent limit A cap on room cost; a higher room can reduce other payouts too
Co-pay The share of an approved claim you pay yourself
Deductible The amount you pay before the insurer pays
Network hospital A hospital that has an arrangement with the insurer for cashless claims
Exclusions What the policy does not cover
Before you buy
Disclose your full medical history honestly.
Check waiting periods, limits and sub-limits, not only the premium.
Check whether nearby hospitals are in the network.
Renew on time so that you do not lose continuity benefits.
Talking it through with Moneytec
You can list your existing life and health policies and go through them with Gulshan Kohli. He is a Kotak Life advisor; ask him what is available for your situation before you decide.
Insurance is the subject matter of solicitation. Benefits and exclusions differ by policy, so read the policy wording before you buy.

## Mutual Fund KYC: Documents, Process & Status | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/mutual-fund-kyc

KYC (Know Your Customer) is an identity and address check that you complete before investing in mutual funds in India. It is done once and works across fund houses, mostly online. Documents you usually need
PAN
Aadhaar, or a passport for NRIs
A bank account in your name
A photo
How the process works
Fill in your details through a fund house, a KRA or your distributor.
Verify your identity, commonly through Aadhaar-based verification and an in-person or video check.
Sign digitally and submit.
The KYC Registration Agency (KRA) records your status, and fund houses can then rely on it.
What your KYC status means
Status What it generally means
Validated Your records have been verified and you can generally invest across fund houses
Registered You can generally continue, but a fresh check may be needed for a new fund house
On hold or rejected Something needs to be corrected before you can invest
You can check your status on a KRA website using your PAN. Status names can change, so ask if you are not sure what yours means.
When you may need to update it
Your name, address, mobile number or email has changed.
Your PAN and Aadhaar need linking.
You have become an NRI or have returned to India.
KYC for NRIs
NRIs usually need a passport and overseas address proof along with PAN, plus FATCA details. See the NRI investment guide .
Never share your OTP or banking passwords with anyone for KYC, including a distributor. Moneytec never collects your investment money.

## Mutual Fund Terms: NAV, CAGR, AMC, Exit Load | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/mutual-fund-terms

Every term you will see on Moneytec and in most scheme documents, explained in plain English. The basics
Term Meaning
AMC Asset Management Company: the fund house that runs a mutual fund.
Scheme A specific mutual fund, with its own objective and portfolio.
Unit Your share in a scheme.
NAV Net Asset Value: the price of one unit, usually declared each business day.
Redemption Selling your units back to get your money.
Folio Your account number with a fund house.
Nominee The person you name to receive your investments if you die.
Ways of investing
Term Meaning
SIP Systematic Investment Plan: a fixed amount invested regularly.
Lump sum Investing a single larger amount at once.
STP Systematic Transfer Plan: moving money regularly from one scheme to another.
SWP Systematic Withdrawal Plan: withdrawing a set amount regularly.
Step-up SIP A SIP whose amount rises at set intervals.
Growth option Gains stay invested and are reflected in the NAV.
IDCW option Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal: payouts that may be made from the scheme, and which reduce the NAV.
Returns and costs
Term Meaning
CAGR Compound Annual Growth Rate: a smoothed yearly growth rate between two points. Real returns are uneven.
XIRR A yearly return calculation for several cash flows at different dates, such as a SIP.
Expense ratio The scheme’s yearly cost as a percentage of its assets, already reflected in the NAV.
Exit load A charge some schemes apply if you redeem within a set period.
Riskometer A scale from Low to Very High that shows a scheme’s risk level.
Benchmark An index that a scheme’s performance is compared with.
Inflation The general rise in prices, which reduces what money can buy.
Fund types and plans
Term Meaning
Equity fund Invests mainly in company shares.
Debt fund Invests mainly in bonds and money-market instruments.
Hybrid fund Invests in a mix of equity and debt.
ELSS Equity Linked Savings Scheme: an equity fund with a 3-year lock-in.
Index fund Aims to follow a market index.
Direct plan You invest without a distributor; lower expense ratio.
Regular plan You invest through a distributor, who earns commission; higher expense ratio.
People, rules and accounts
Term Meaning
SEBI Securities and Exchange Board of India: the regulator for mutual funds.
AMFI Association of Mutual Funds in India: the industry body that registers distributors.
ARN AMFI Registration Number: a distributor’s registration. Gulshan Kohli’s is ARN-105840.
IRDAI Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India: the insurance regulator.
KYC Know Your Customer: the identity check you complete before investing.
PAN Permanent Account Number: your income-tax ID, needed to invest.
NRI Non-Resident Indian.
NRE account A rupee account generally used for money earned outside India.
NRO account A rupee account generally used for income earned in India.
FATCA A tax-residency declaration required when you invest.

## Mutual Fund Portfolio Review: What to Check | Moneytec
Source: https://moneytec.in/portfolio-review

A portfolio review is a regular check that your SIPs and funds still fit your goals, timeline and comfort with risk. It often means organising what you have, not replacing everything. What gets checked
Goals: is each investment linked to a purpose and date?
Progress: are you on track at your current amount?
Risk: does the overall mix still suit you, especially as a goal gets close?
Overlap: do several funds hold much the same investments?
Number of funds: can you track what you hold?
Costs: expense ratios and any exit loads.
Performance in context: against its benchmark and similar funds over longer periods, not just the last few months.
Paperwork: nominee, KYC, bank and contact details.
What to bring
A Consolidated Account Statement (CAS), which shows your mutual fund holdings in one place
Your list of SIPs
Your goals and when you need the money
Any large upcoming expenses
How often?
Many people review once a year, and also when something big changes, such as a new job, marriage, a child, a home loan or a move abroad. Checking every week usually makes market noise feel more important than it is.
Before you switch anything
Switching is treated as selling one fund and buying another. It can trigger tax and an exit load, and ELSS instalments cannot be redeemed until their 3-year lock-in ends. A recent dip alone is not always a reason to change.
How Moneytec helps
Gulshan Kohli can go through your existing SIPs and funds with you and organise them around your goals, timeline and comfort with risk. Any decision and payment stays with you, through the fund house.
